rationale: Probability an exposed credential still authenticates somewhere at the time of use. Bounded below by rotation and forced resets after disclosure; bounded above by measured password reuse. The low end assumes most credentials in older corpora are dead; the high end assumes reuse at the rate observed in leaked-credential analyses rather than the higher rate people self-report.
source: Reuse measured on leaked credentials ~40% (Pearman et al. and successors); infostealer telemetry shows a median 49% of a user's passwords distinct from one another; self-reported reuse runs 75-93% and is not used here because self-report overstates.

rationale: Probability an exposed credential is actually tried against some service within a year. Credential stuffing is industrialised and dumped combolists are swept broadly rather than selectively, so the high end is 1. The low end allows for corpora that circulate narrowly or are never operationalised.
source: Credential stuffing is a median 19% of all authentication attempts in SSO provider logs; 76% of organisations report an account takeover in a 12-month period.

rationale: Probability the targeted account is not protected by a second factor that blocks a valid stolen password. The low end reflects institutional accounts on parliamentary systems where MFA is increasingly mandated; the high end reflects personal consumer accounts, where adoption is far lower. Note this parameter does NOT protect against stealer-log compromise, which captures session cookies and bypasses the second factor entirely.
source: Enterprise MFA adoption is materially higher than consumer; session-cookie theft by infostealers authenticates without invoking a second factor, which is why the stealer floor is estimated separately rather than passed through this link.
